questions.question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

The family's meeting on property dispute begins today and I'm just sitting down with a cup of coffee, enjoying _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The calm before the storm**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Idiom **is a collection of words established by usage as having a meaning distinct from the meanings of the individual words
 
• The Idiom** the calm before the storm** means a quiet or peaceful period preceding a period of intense activity, argument, or difficulty.
 
• *Example *: My mother's silence feels like** the calm before the storm.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The phrase **the bottom line** means the primary and most important factor

*Example *:** The bottom line** of this class is completing assignment.

 
• The phrase** the batter of **means strike over and over with difficult blows.

*Example *: A detainee was **battered to** death with a table leg

 
• The phrase **the corridors of power** means places where individuals talk about issues and make imperative choices particularly about political things.

*Example *:**The corridors of power** in New Delhi is Supreme court.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

How did you __come about__ his purse?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Come by**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The above underlined phrase can be substituted with **come by instead of come about.**
 
• The word **about as an adverb **is used to denote movement within a given area.

​*Example *: Tell me something **about **yourself.

 
• The word** by as a preposition** is used for indicating a method of accomplishing something.

*Example* : Can you please stand **by**?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• An **adverb **is a word or phrase that modifies or qualifies an adjective, verb, other adverb, or a word group, expressing a relationship of place, time, circumstance, manner, cause, degree, and so on (e.g., gently, quite, then, there ).

*Example *: Quickly, slowly, yesterday, last week, here, there, today, daily, never, rarely, extremely, annually, etc.

 
• A **preposition **is a word that governs and usually comes before a noun or pronoun and expresses a relationship to another word or element in the clause.

*Example *: in, at, on, of, to.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

She is / the very ambitious woman / I have ever / come across.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is The very ambitious women.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The segment that contains the error is 'the very ambitious women'.
 
• The word 'very' has been incorrectly used as 'very' is used before adverbs and adjectives to add emphasis. It means ‘to a great degree’.
 
 
• Example: He drives very fast.
 
 
 
• 'Very' is not used before the superlatives which use the 'most'.
 
• The superlative degree of comparison is the highest degree of comparison.It shows which of these nouns being compared has the greatest degree of the mentioned quality or qualities.
 
• The superlative degree of ‘ambitious’ is ‘most ambitious’.
 
• Therefore the use of ‘the very ambitious woman’ should be replaced with ‘the most ambitious woman’ to make it grammatically correct.
 
• Thus, option 3 is the correct answer.

 

Correct sentence: She is the most ambitious woman I have ever come across.

questions.question:

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __am not afraid to speak__

__
 
• In the above sentence there should be speak instead of spoke.
 
• The word spoke is past tense of word Speak.
 
• The word speak means to say something.
 
• The above sentence is in present tense hence the word speak should be used.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**Tenses Chart**

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
**Tenses**

 
 
 
**Rules and Formula**

 
 
 

 
 
**Simple Present Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Verb in the base form/third person plural form + the rest of the sentence**

 
 
 

 
 
**Present Continuous Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Helping Verb(am/is/are) + Main verb + ing + the rest of the sentence **

 
 
 

 
 
**Present Perfect Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Helping Verb (have/has) + Past participle of the main verb + the rest of the sentence along with the time frame**

 
 
 

 
 
**Present Perfect Continuous Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Have/Has + Been + Verb+ ing + the rest of the sentence**

 
 
 

 
 
**Simple Past Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Verb + ed / verb in the past tense + the rest of the sentence**

 
 
 

 
 
**Past Continuous Tense **

 
 
 
**Subject + Helping Verb(was/were) + Main verb + ing + the rest of the sentence**

 
 
 

 
 
**Past Perfect Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Helping Verb (had) + Past participle of the main verb + the rest of the sentence along with the time frame.**

 
 
 

 
 
**Past Perfect Continuous Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + Had + Been + Verb + ing + the rest of the sentence**

 
 
 

 
 
**Simple Future Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object**

 
 
 

 
 
**Future Continuous Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + will be/shall be + V1 + ing + Object**

 
 
 

 
 
**Future Perfect Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + will have/shall have + V3 + Object**

 
 
 

 
 
**Future Perfect Continuous Tense**

 
 
 
**Subject + will have been + V1 + ing + Object**

Subject + Helping Verb(was/were) + Main verb + ing + the rest of the sentence

 
 
 

 
 
Past Perfect Tense

 
 
 
Subject + Helping Verb (had) + Past participle of the main verb + the rest of the sentence along with the time frame.

 
 
 

 
 
Past Perfect Continuous Tense

 
 
 
Subject + Had + Been + Verb + ing + the rest of the sentence

 
 
 

 
 
Simple Future Tense

 
 
 
Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object

 
 
 

 
 
Future Continuous Tense

 
 
 
Subject + will be/shall be + V1 + ing + Object

 
 
 

 
 
Future Perfect Tense

 
 
 
Subject + will have/shall have + V3 + Object

 
 
 

 
 
Future Perfect Continuous Tense

 
 
 
Subject + will have been + V1 + ing + Object

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

He was enough tall / to be admitted / into the armed forces.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "He was enough tall". 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Enough means 'as much as necessary'.
 
• It can be used with an adjective, an adverb, a verb or a noun. It can also act as a pronoun.
 
 
• **With adjectives and adverbs : enough comes after adjectives and adverbs**.
 
 
• For example: I'm not tall enough to reach the top shelf.
 
• For example: Your marks are good enough to study engineering at university.
 
 
 
 
 
• From the above explanation it can be concluded that the correct sentence is: He was tall enough to be admitted into the armed forces. 

Therefore, the correct answer is "Option 4".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• With verbs: enough comes after verbs.
 
 
• For example: I make sure I drink enough during the day.
 
 
 
• With nouns: enough comes before nouns.
 
 
• For example: There isn't enough bread to make sandwiches.
 
 
 
• As a pronoun: enough can also be used without a noun. 
 
 
• For example: I'll get some more chairs. There aren't enough.
 
 
 
• With an adjective and a noun: When enough is used with an adjective and a noun, two positions are possible but the meaning changes.
 
 
• We haven't got big enough envelopes. 
 
• We haven't got enough big envelopes.
 
 
 
• When enough is after the adjective (big enough envelopes), it describes the adjective – the envelopes are too small.
 
• When enough is before the adjective (enough big envelopes), it describes the noun phrase – we have some big envelopes, but we need more.
